title: Evening letting go
tomorrow: why would a prophet tell people to put out the lamps at night?

cards: Some worries earn their keep. The one about money makes you open the budget; the one about a test makes you study. Then it climbs into bed with you, and at midnight it's still talking, though it has nothing new to say.
Can you put it down? The Buddha told a story about a man and a raft, and it answers with a question. A man comes to a great stretch of water.
This shore is dangerous. The far shore is safe. There's no boat and no bridge.

teach.h: A RAFT OF GRASS AND BRANCHES.
teach.b: So he gathers grass, sticks and branches, binds them into a raft, and paddles across with his hands and feet.
On the far side he thinks: this raft was so useful, I'll lift it onto my head and carry it wherever I go. Should he? The monks say no.
Leave it on the shore and walk on, the Buddha says. I have taught you the Dhamma like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on. Here's the debate, and both sides are Buddhist readers.
One side says: the raft stands for everything, even the teachings.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: LET GO OF EVEN GOOD THINGS.
teach.b: The same sutta says even good things are to be let go, how much more the bad ones.

teach.h: THE OTHER: USE IT ALL THE WAY ACROSS.
teach.b: Once you're across, carry nothing. The other side says: look at the order. He doesn't drop the raft in the middle of the river.
He uses it all the way across. Let go too early and you don't arrive; you sink. Both sides agree on the teaching at the center: non-clinging.
What carries you is for crossing, not for wearing on your head.
A worry can be a raft. Use it to get across: make the call, write the plan. Then pull it up on the shore.
Carrying it into bed is carrying the raft.

how: Buddhist teachers use the Buddha's raft simile to teach non-clinging: the teachings are to be used for crossing, not held onto for their own sake.

o: forgetting what happened today as fast as you can
staying up until every problem has an answer
setting the day's load down once it has done its job

p: clinging to what already did its job
for crossing over, not for holding on

s: the Buddha told the man to carry the raft with him out of gratitude
he says to leave it on the shore and walk on.
the parable says even good things are for crossing, not clinging
the same sutta says even good states are to be let go, how much more the bad ones.
letting go, in the parable, means never building a raft at all
he needed the raft to cross. the question is what he does with it afterward.

games.q: your friend says the raft means you should drop even the Buddha's teachings right now. what's the best case for the other reading?
o: the man uses the raft all the way across before he sets it down.
the Buddha warns that building rafts is itself a kind of clinging.
the far shore is imaginary, so the raft never really mattered.
games.why: both readings agree the raft is for crossing, not carrying. the other side's point is timing: you don't drop it in the middle of the river.

practice: Write the worry on a scrap of paper in one line, and under it the one step it's asking for, if there is one. Fold the paper and set it down somewhere away from your bed. Then let your hands rest open and empty while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Evening letting go: using what got you across today, then setting it down on the shore before sleep, the way the Buddha's man leaves the raft.

carryVoice: Here's the line: put it down, once it has carried you all the way across. Day done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft: for crossing over, not for grasping; even good states are to be abandoned, how much more bad ones)
